newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-France hikes company taxes to meet EMU goal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-France hikes company taxes to meet EMU goal.

text.p: France's leftist government raised taxes on big business on Monday to bring down this year's public deficit, found by an audit to be running well above the level required to qualify for a single European currency.

The audit ordered by Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin on taking office last month showed the 1997 deficit was running at 3.5 to 3.7 percent of gross domestic product, significantly beyond the three percent limit set by the Maastricht treaty.

Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said that to meet the target for the euro, the government would cut the deficit by 32 billion francs ($5.3 billion), with 22 billion in higher taxes on companies' profits and capital gains, and 10 billion in spending cuts.

The measures won endorsement from Germany, Paris' chief partner in the drive to launch economic and monetary union in 1999. Finance Minister Theo Waigel saying the French were doing their best to meet the Maastricht target.

Strauss-Kahn, who telephoned Waigel before announcing his measures, refused to set a numerical deficit target for 1997, the reference year to qualify for economic and monetary union (EMU) but said the measures "concern 0.4 percent of GDP".
"Less would have been insufficient, more would have blocked economic growth," he told a news conference.
France would meet the Maastricht treaty criteria "in the same conditions as its (European Union) partners", he said.
Economists said the measures announced should bring down the 1997 deficit to about 3.2 percent of GDP, sufficient to qualify for the euro.
In line with Jospin's pledge that there would be "no new austerity plan" to qualify for EMU, the package contained no tax increase on households.
The defence budget will bear two billion francs of this year's 10 billion spending cuts.

Arguing that company profits were at a record high, and that previous centre-right governments had given industry tax breaks and subsidies, Strauss-Kahn announced a 15 percent increase in company tax in 1997 and 1998 falling to 10 percent in 1999.

The increases are calculated on the 33.3 percent basic rate of company tax. Since 1995, there has been a 10 percent surtax and the rate stands currently at 36.6 percent. Corporate capital gains will be taxed at the same rate as profits.
Small firms and loss-making companies were exempted from the increase.
The government said it was facing a tax shortfall this year of 15 to 17 billion francs and a public spending overshoot of 12 to 20 billion francs.
In addition, the welfare deficit in the main social security fund was running at 35 to 38 billion francs, compared with the 30.4 billion francs target initially forecast.

Speaking in Munich shortly before Strauss-Kahn's statement, Waigel said the French were aware of their responsibilities and the tax rises were genuine measures, not creative accountancy, even though they should be followed by structural reforms.
Economists said the tax package was slightly bigger than expected but its concentration on big business was predictable.

"It is the corporate sector that takes the pain. The overall impact is slightly larger than people had been expecting. All this is wholly coherent with the extremely Keynesian approach of the government," said Christopher Potts, an economist at Paris brokers Cheuvreux de Virieu.
The centre-right opposition, ousted from government in a June 1 parliamentary election upset, attacked the government's emphasis on taxing business rather than cutting spending.

"The economic choices of the government go against the liberal policies which, throughout the world, allow growth and employment, via cuts in state spending, lower taxes and privatisations," said Alain Madelin, leader of the right-wing Liberal Democracy party.
"You can't be part of the euro game by swimming against the European tide," he said. $= 6.041 French Francs)
